newsitem.title: JORDAN: INTERVIEW -- Jordan mulls big stock market sell-offs.
newsitem.headline: INTERVIEW -- Jordan mulls big stock market sell-offs.

text.p: Jordan's stock market is advising the government on plans for a major state sell-off of its extensive stock portfolio as part of a stepped up privatisation effort, its director said on Wednesday.

"The government is now consulting the Amman Financial Market on technical procedures for unloading further investments...we will be giving them some ideas," Wahib al-Shair, director general of the Amman Financial Market, told Reuters.
"We also know the government is considering unloading some or much of its holdings in the market...this ought to provide a larger float for the interested investors," Shair added.

A key element in Jordan's so far slow privatisation effort is state sell-offs of the government's extensive stock holdings -- nearly 35 percent of the bourse's total market capitalisation of 3.5 billion dinars.

Stakes in over 70 out of 135 listed stocks held by its investment arm and state pension funds range from minimal shareholdings in hardly traded firms to a 69.3 percent of blue chip Jordan Phosphate Mines.
Shair said the AMF would enlist international financial expertise on ways of offloading sizeable government holdings.
"We would like to enlist the expertise available abroad...we do not want to reinvent the wheel," he said.
Shair said a government move to implement in 1997 its privatisation pledge, an essential component of IMF directed economic reforms, will give the market a major boost.

"The commitment has not changed, it's the implementation...I see the government moving ahead faster than last year...there is certainly activity towards more privatisation," said Shair, who is also a member of a top privatisation body headed by the prime minister that formulates policy.
Shair said foreign funds were looking for signs of progress on Jordan's privatisation before they could be enticed into further investment.

He said foreigners who complain of a lack of stock availability will see more depth to the market after state selloffs, and listings of 15 newly established firms which he expected to take place later this year.
Funds say with one third of the market already held by mostly Arab investors and a 50 percent foreign ownership ceiling there is insufficient supply of popular bluechips.
Global funds' stake on the bourse stood at end of 1996 at just 1.5 percent of the market's capitalisation against 33 percent held by non-Jordanian Arab investors.
The rest is held by the government and Jordanian investors.

Shair said the new firms, with a combined 70 million to 80 million dinar ($100 million to $110 million) capital, would bring the number of listed firms in the combined official and parallel markets to 150 by year end.
Shair said he was encouraged by a trend in foreign purchases of bluechips which is showing signs of picking up.
"Every month, foreign funds are increasing their purchases...it is certainly continuous and persistent, although not snowballing, and we are still speaking of small numbers."
Jordanian investment managers are saying Middle East funds, which include Jordan as a main component, and global funds have been increasing their activity since December.
Shair said he was hopeful that state selloffs and healthy corporate earnings forecasts would help the market's performance in 1997 surpass last year's disappointing falls.
A new companies law which encourages capital hikes and a new securities law that brings major internal reforms along with automated trading will raise the market's investor profile.
"During the last ten weeks the market has gone up by about eight percent and average daily volume has doubled...and also we are hearing that companies are reporting better profits," he said.
